title: When You'll Believe Anything
coreMove: Leave messy outcomes partly unexplained instead of rushing into a neat story.
sourcePressure: People crave tidy narratives when markets and life are random, complex, and uncertain.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating a confident explanation as proof that the explanation is true.

hook: opening with a generic paycheck scene
opening with a moral lesson about discipline
opening When You'll Believe Anything with a swapped-in personal finance anecdote
counterintuition: reducing When You'll Believe Anything to common-sense advice
tryThisNow: write down your values for ninety seconds
asking for a generic money reflection instead of the narrative move
examples: reusing visible anchors from adjacent chapters instead of narrative and uncertainty

exampleSpecs.domain: a market newsletter writer resisting a tidy explanation for a sudden selloff
exampleSpecs.audience: a writer whose readers reward certainty
exampleSpecs.stakes: a neat story may teach false precision and bad trades
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he publishes three plausible causes and one honest unknown instead of one heroic headline
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a draft newsletter headline with five deleted explanations beneath it

exampleSpecs.domain: a baseball analyst refusing to explain a slump with one clubhouse rumor
exampleSpecs.audience: an analyst protecting uncertainty in public commentary
exampleSpecs.stakes: fans may mistake narrative neatness for evidence
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she asks which data would be true if the rumor were false before saying it on air
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a broadcast desk stat sheet beside a rumor text

exampleSpecs.domain: a supply manager investigating why a shipment arrived late
exampleSpecs.audience: a manager avoiding the first clean story from a vendor
exampleSpecs.stakes: punishing the wrong cause leaves the real risk untouched
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she keeps the timeline open until port logs, customs delay, and warehouse staffing are all visible
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a shipment timeline with three colored delay bands

exampleSpecs.domain: a family explaining a relative's bankruptcy without reducing it to laziness
exampleSpecs.audience: a sibling preserving complexity when shame wants a simple label
exampleSpecs.stakes: a tidy blame story can block useful support and repeat the mistake
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she writes income loss, medical bills, pride, and timing in separate columns before speaking at dinner
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a folded bankruptcy notice beside a legal pad with four columns

exampleSpecs.domain: a climate startup board explaining a failed pilot to investors
exampleSpecs.audience: a board chair resisting one villain story
exampleSpecs.stakes: a clean villain may hide technical and market uncertainty the next pilot must face
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she replaces the blame slide with a map of assumptions that proved false at different times
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a slide deck with the word assumptions typed across the top

exampleSpecs.domain: a judge reviewing sentencing reports where one incident dominates the narrative
exampleSpecs.audience: a judge aware that coherent stories can outrun messy evidence
exampleSpecs.stakes: a person's future may turn on which story sounds neatest
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she rereads the full timeline after noticing the report's opening anecdote has taken over her attention
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a sentencing report flagged with colored tabs along the edge
